title: Peak into the Past: An Archaeo-Astronomy Summer School
extended_summary:
This paper describes the design, delivery, and perceived impact of an archaeo-astronomy summer school intended to support transition from primary to secondary school and to enrich STEM learning through outdoor, interdisciplinary activities. The authors aim to show how local heritage sites can be used as outdoor classrooms to engage pupils with astronomy, archaeology, ecology, citizenship, and related science and mathematics concepts.

The intervention was a five-day summer school in 2009 run with The Meden School and Technology College in Worksop. Twenty-seven gifted and talented pupils from Years 5-8 participated. Activities were split between school-based preparation, field visits to two Peak District monuments (Arbor Low and Nine Ladies), analysis workshops at Nottingham Trent University, and a final presentation day for parents. Students conducted practical investigations such as surveying, sampling ecology, estimating construction effort, using planetarium software, and learning archaeological interpretation.

The paper reports mainly descriptive evidence of impact: student presentations, reflections, and follow-up activities suggested increased confidence, retention of knowledge, stronger subject understanding, and successful engagement with interdisciplinary content. The authors conclude that archaeo-astronomy can be integrated into the curriculum and that outdoor learning with local heritage sites can support both student learning and teacher development.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive practitioner article in a school science magazine, not a controlled study. It reports outcomes anecdotally and does not provide a formal evaluation design, comparison group, or statistical analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The program appears beneficial for the participating gifted and talented students, but the evidence is qualitative and lacks quantified effect sizes. Impact is promising but unclear for general K-12 populations, so it fits a yellow tier.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the archaeo-astronomy summer school improved students’ ability to apply scientific ideas in context, including using Stellarium, compasses, sampling, and measurement to test hypotheses about monument alignment and site ecology. The evidence is descriptive and qualitative rather than experimental, with the authors stating that pupils achieved all predefined outcomes and demonstrated better understanding of misconceptions such as the Sun’s rising/setting positions.
finding.measure: Student presentations, fieldwork products, and teacher/researcher observation of conceptual understanding and application of astronomy/ecology methods

finding.finding_summary: The summer school had positive impacts on interdisciplinary subject learning in archaeology, astronomy, ecology, and citizenship-related content. The authors report that student presentations on the final day showed coverage of all targeted topics and appropriate use of key vocabulary, with some evidence of retained knowledge during a follow-up museum visit more than a year later.
finding.measure: Final-day student presentations, follow-up museum visit observations, and use of topic-specific vocabulary/knowledge

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes improved self-confidence, motivation, and enjoyment among participants, especially in the initial focus group and during presentation activities. The evidence is qualitative: students were described as becoming more confident, more engaged, and better able to reflect on their work through the wiki and public presentations.
finding.measure: Observed student confidence, engagement, and willingness to present/reflection activities

finding.finding_summary: The project appears to strengthen collaboration, communication, and presentation skills through group fieldwork, creative displays, poetry, theatre, and PowerPoint presentations. The authors explicitly note improvements in social skills and individual growth, and the follow-up wiki work supported reflection and communication over time.
finding.measure: Student collaboration, presentations, reflective wiki use, and teacher/researcher observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the wiki and supporting resources made it easier for teachers to maintain contact, monitor progress, and run follow-up work without requiring repeated specialist visits. This is presented as a practical benefit for delivery and sustainability of the enrichment program rather than as a measured workload outcome.
finding.measure: Described teacher coordination/support needs and sustainability of follow-up activities via wiki
